title: Ring's AI-Powered Drone Automatically Patrols Inside Your Home
content:
Ring’s AI-Powered Drone Automatically Patrols Inside Your Home
Home security can now fly. Amazon-owned Ring has announced the Ring Drone Cam, a $250 indoor flying security camera designed to automatically patrol a home’s interior.
The AI-powered Ring Drone Cam works alongside existing Ring products, including static cameras and sensors. When an alarm sounds or motion is detected, the drone automatically deploys to investigate.
Homeowners can also launch the drone on command or program custom flight routines on a scheduled basis. Due to its compact, lightweight design, flight times are limited to eight minutes per charge. Users can monitor a live 360-degree feed on their smartphones while the drone is airborne, and built-in LED spotlights allow it to operate effectively in total darkness.
Although designed to operate autonomously, initial setup requires some manual effort: users must carry the drone throughout their home to help it build an internal spatial map. Additionally, Ring notes that navigation works best in environments with distinct visual details; reflective surfaces, featureless walls, and frameless glass may pose operational challenges.
Detailed camera specifications remain sparse, but Ring confirms the drone features a 2K (1920×1920) square image sensor paired with a 148-degree field of view.
After completing a patrol, the drone automatically returns to its base station, fully recharging in roughly an hour. Ring emphasizes that all video and audio recording automatically stops whenever the drone is docked.
With a subscription, users can store, share, and review recorded footage—including motion events and Live View feeds—for up to 180 days. Users can also search through archival footage using plain-text queries.
Designed exclusively for indoor use, the premise behind the Ring Drone Cam is simple: a single autonomous drone can monitor the same space as multiple stationary security cameras.
Ring founder Jamie Siminoff told The Verge during a launch event that the company has spent a decade developing the drone off and on, only recently achieving its design and performance goals after returning to the drawing board a year ago.
Although Amazon’s listing notes the device has not yet received FCC authorization, Siminoff states that the U.S.-assembled drone complies with all regulatory standards.
The Ring Drone Cam is scheduled to ship in January 2027 for $249.99.

report.summary: Ring has unveiled a $250 AI-powered indoor security drone that launches automatically when alarms trigger, streams live 2K 360-degree video, and launches in January 2027.
report.background: Ring built its business on doorbells and static outdoor cameras, then expanded into indoor cams, alarm sensors, and subscription-backed cloud recording. A flying camera is the natural next step: instead of blanketing a house with fixed cameras, one drone could cover the same ground and physically move toward a disturbance. The concept has circulated for years—Amazon even patented a 'drone-as-security-camera' idea in 2018—but battery life, indoor navigation, and cost kept it theoretical. Recent advances in SLAM (simultaneous localization and mapping), tiny 2K sensors, and on-device AI made a consumer product feasible, and Ring says it spent a decade off and on in development. The launch also lands amid growing scrutiny of home surveillance: privacy groups worry about always-on sensing inside private spaces, and Ring notes the device has not yet received FCC authorization. Pricing sits well above a single indoor camera but below a multi-camera setup, framing the drone as a replacement for several stationary units.
key_points: The Ring Drone Cam costs $249.99 and ships in January 2027. It works alongside existing Ring cameras and sensors, deploying automatically when an alarm sounds or motion is detected—or on a homeowner's command or a scheduled flight routine.

Flight time is limited to about eight minutes per charge because the drone is small and light. After a patrol it returns to a base station and recharges in roughly an hour, and Ring says recording fully stops while docked.
Video comes from a 2K square (1920x1920) sensor with a 148-degree field of view, streamed live to a phone as a 360-degree feed. Built-in LED spotlights let it see in total darkness.

Setup requires manually carrying the drone around the home to build a spatial map, and navigation works best where walls have distinct visual features—mirrors, blank walls, and frameless glass can confuse it.

A subscription unlocks cloud storage, sharing, and review of footage for up to 180 days, plus plain-text search across recorded video. Amazon's listing notes the device has not yet received FCC authorization, though Ring says it meets all standards.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the Ring Drone Cam is a concrete test of embodied AI in the home: indoor SLAM, autonomous navigation, and edge inference packed into a sub-$300 consumer device. Success would validate cheap visual mapping and push competitors toward mobile sensing rather than fixed cameras. For developers, it signals demand for robust indoor autonomy stacks—visual-inertial odometry, obstacle avoidance, and lightweight AI models that run on battery-constrained hardware—and it may open an API or subscription ecosystem for third-party automations. For regular users, the appeal is one device covering multiple rooms and actively investigating alerts instead of passively watching. The trade-offs are real: eight-minute flights, a setup chore, blind spots on reflective surfaces, and deeper privacy questions about a camera that flies through bedrooms. Regulatory approval also remains pending.
report.tools: To explore the underlying tech, look at Frigate NVR and Home Assistant for local, subscription-free camera automation; ROS 2 with VINS-Fusion or ORB-SLAM3 for indoor visual mapping; PX4 and ArduPilot for drone flight control; and YOLO or NanoDet for lightweight on-device object detection. For privacy-minded alternatives, ESPHome and OpenCV-based DIY patrol robots are worth watching as the open-source analogue to Ring's closed ecosystem.
